cards.statement: React interprets a capitalized JSX tag as a reference to a component function.
cards.explanation: A tag such as <Profile /> refers to the Profile component; lowercase tags represent built-in elements.

cards.statement: Defining a component inside another component preserves its identity across parent renders.
cards.explanation: A nested definition creates a new component function when the parent renders. React treats it as a different component, which can reset its state.
cards.misconception: A nested component definition retains its identity between parent renders.

cards.statement: A named component export is imported with a bare identifier after import.
cards.explanation: A named component export uses a named import such as import { Profile } from './Profile.js'. A bare identifier imports a default export.
cards.misconception: Named and default component exports use the same import syntax.

cards.statement: A component returning sibling JSX elements groups them under a single root.
cards.explanation: JSX needs one enclosing element or Fragment when a component returns several sibling elements.

cards.statement: A Fragment groups sibling JSX elements and renders their DOM nodes directly.
cards.explanation: A Fragment provides a JSX parent while adding no wrapper element to the browser's DOM tree.

cards.statement: JSX accepts an unclosed tag when the browser treats it as a void element.
cards.explanation: JSX requires explicit closing syntax, including for a self-closing tag.
cards.misconception: HTML's void-element syntax works unchanged in JSX.

cards.statement: In JSX, the SVG stroke-width attribute is written as strokeWidth.
cards.explanation: Many HTML and SVG attributes use camelCase in JSX because their names become JavaScript object keys.

cards.statement: A JSX element uses the HTML class attribute to assign a CSS class to a DOM node.
cards.explanation: React uses className in JSX for a DOM element's CSS class.
cards.misconception: The HTML class attribute keeps the same name in JSX.

cards.statement: JSX reads a JavaScript expression placed between curly braces as element content.
cards.explanation: Inside a JSX tag, {name} inserts the value of the JavaScript expression name into the rendered content.

source.title: JavaScript in JSX with Curly Braces

cards.statement: JSX expects a CSS declaration string in a DOM element's style prop.
cards.explanation: The JSX style prop takes a JavaScript object, such as style={{ backgroundColor: 'black' }}.
cards.misconception: Inline styles in JSX use the same declaration string as HTML.

source.title: JavaScript in JSX with Curly Braces

cards.statement: A function component can return null to omit its UI for a condition.
cards.explanation: Returning null tells React to render nothing for that component in the selected branch.

cards.statement: In JSX, count && <Badge /> hides the expression when count is 0.
cards.explanation: When count is 0, the && expression evaluates to 0, and React renders that 0. Use a boolean condition such as count > 0.
cards.misconception: A falsy number on the left of && disappears from JSX.

cards.statement: A parent passes a prop to a child component through an attribute on the child's JSX tag.
cards.explanation: The parent supplies values such as <Avatar size={100} />, and the child reads them from its props.

cards.statement: A function component receives each JSX prop as a separate positional argument.
cards.explanation: React supplies a single props object to a function component. The component can read its properties or destructure them.
cards.misconception: React calls a component with one function argument per prop.

cards.statement: A component can destructure named props in its function parameter.
cards.explanation: A declaration such as function Avatar({ person, size }) reads those properties from the props object.

cards.statement: A destructured prop default replaces null with the fallback value.
cards.explanation: A default parameter value applies when the prop is missing or undefined. An explicit null remains null.
cards.misconception: Destructuring defaults treat null like an omitted prop.

cards.statement: Nested JSX inside a custom component becomes that component's children prop.
cards.explanation: For <Card><Avatar /></Card>, Card receives <Avatar /> as its children prop and can choose where to render it.

cards.statement: A child component can edit the props object it receives to update its parent.
cards.explanation: Props are read-only snapshots. To change what a child receives, its parent supplies new prop values on a later render.
cards.misconception: Mutating received props communicates a change back to the parent.

cards.statement: A parent can pass a callback function as a prop for a child to call during an interaction.
cards.explanation: Custom component props can hold JavaScript functions, letting a child call behavior supplied by its parent.

cards.statement: JSX spread can forward a component's received props to a child.
cards.explanation: Writing <Avatar {...props} /> passes the properties in props to Avatar.

cards.statement: Custom component props are limited to the attributes supported by DOM elements.
cards.explanation: Your own components can accept prop names you define. Built-in DOM elements have predefined supported props.
cards.misconception: Custom components share the DOM element attribute list.

cards.statement: In React 19, function components receive ref as a regular prop.
cards.explanation: React 19 lets a function component read ref from its props, so forwardRef is no longer needed for that purpose.

cards.statement: In React 19, defaultProps still supplies defaults for function components.
cards.explanation: React 19 removed defaultProps support for function components; use default parameter values instead. Class components still support defaultProps.
cards.misconception: Function components retain defaultProps support in React 19.

cards.statement: In React 19, React runs propTypes checks for function components in development.
cards.explanation: React 19 ignores propTypes checks rather than running them in development.
cards.misconception: React 19 still performs runtime propTypes checks for function components.

cards.statement: Calling root.render(<App />) triggers the initial render of a React tree.
cards.explanation: After createRoot selects a DOM container, calling its render method starts the tree's initial render.

cards.statement: Updating component state queues React to render that component again.
cards.explanation: A state update triggers a later render so React can calculate the UI from the updated state.

cards.statement: During rendering, React calls component functions to determine their JSX output.
cards.explanation: Rendering is the calculation phase in which React calls components to find out what they return.

cards.statement: React skips child component functions by default when their parent re-renders.
cards.explanation: By default, React renders components nested inside the updated component. Optimizations can skip some of that work.
cards.misconception: Unchanged child props automatically prevent child rendering.

cards.statement: On the initial commit, React appends newly created DOM nodes to the target container.
cards.explanation: React creates DOM nodes for the initial render and places them in the DOM during commit.

cards.statement: React changes the DOM after a re-render even when the rendered output stays the same.
cards.explanation: React leaves DOM nodes alone when a re-render produces the same output as the previous render.
cards.misconception: Every React re-render forces a matching DOM update.

cards.statement: The render tree keeps the same component shape across conditional branches.
cards.explanation: Conditional rendering can put different child components in the render tree on different render passes.
cards.misconception: A React render tree has a fixed shape regardless of rendered conditions.

source.title: Understanding Your UI as a Tree

cards.statement: A module dependency tree includes imported utility modules alongside component modules.
cards.explanation: Each node represents a module, including modules containing functions or constants rather than components.

source.title: Understanding Your UI as a Tree

cards.statement: A pure component may return different JSX from the same props, state, and context.
cards.explanation: A pure component returns the same JSX for the same inputs. React relies on that predictable calculation.
cards.misconception: Changing output for identical inputs is compatible with render purity.

source.title: Components and Hooks must be pure

cards.statement: A component can push items into an array it creates during that same render.
cards.explanation: Mutating an array created within the current render is local mutation; the array starts fresh on the next render.

cards.statement: An array created before rendering can safely accumulate JSX across component renders.
cards.explanation: Appending JSX to a preexisting array during render changes a nonlocal value and can duplicate items on later renders.
cards.misconception: Mutating a shared array during render is equivalent to local mutation.

cards.statement: A component's render phase can send an analytics event as part of its JSX calculation.
cards.explanation: Sending an analytics event is a side effect. Render must stay free of side effects because React can run the calculation again.
cards.misconception: External writes are safe while calculating JSX.

source.title: Components and Hooks must be pure

cards.statement: useState returns the current state value and a setter function for requesting its next value.
cards.explanation: The two-item array from useState contains the value for the current render and its corresponding set function.

cards.statement: A local variable in a function component persists between renders like useState data.
cards.explanation: React runs the component function again on a re-render, recreating its local variables. useState retains data between renders.
cards.misconception: Ordinary local variables provide the same component memory as state.

cards.statement: An event handler reads a new state value immediately after calling its state setter.
cards.explanation: A state setter affects the next render. The event handler still reads the state snapshot from the render that created it.
cards.misconception: Calling a state setter mutates the state variable in the running handler.

cards.statement: React batches state updates queued during the same event handler.
cards.explanation: React processes queued updates after the event handler finishes, avoiding a render between its individual setter calls.

source.title: Queueing a Series of State Updates

cards.statement: An updater function receives the pending state produced by earlier updates in the same queue.
cards.explanation: React passes each queued updater the pending value left by the preceding update, then uses its return value for the next one.

source.title: Queueing a Series of State Updates

cards.statement: Passing a plain number to a state setter increments the value already queued for that state.
cards.explanation: A plain value queues a replacement with that value. To calculate from pending state, pass an updater function.
cards.misconception: A numeric setter argument is added to previously queued state.

source.title: Queueing a Series of State Updates

cards.statement: React uses Object.is to decide whether a proposed state value matches the current value.
cards.explanation: When Object.is finds the new value equal to the current state, React skips the update. It may still call the component before skipping its children.

cards.statement: Setting an object state variable with a partial object merges its fields into the prior object.
cards.explanation: A useState setter replaces the object value. Copy the previous fields explicitly, for example with object spread.
cards.misconception: useState merges partial object updates automatically.

cards.statement: Updating a nested object in state involves copying the path to the changed property.
cards.explanation: Object spread is shallow, so an immutable nested update copies the outer object and each nested object along the changed path.

cards.statement: Calling sort() on an array held in state leaves the previous state array intact.
cards.explanation: sort() mutates its array. Copy an array held in state before sorting the copy.
cards.misconception: Array sort() returns a sorted result while preserving the input array.

cards.statement: Passing createItems() to useState defers that call until state initialization.
cards.explanation: JavaScript calls createItems() while evaluating the argument on each render. Passing createItems as an initializer lets React call it during initialization.
cards.misconception: React lazily evaluates a function call passed as the initial state value.

cards.statement: The setter returned by useState keeps the same identity across renders.
cards.explanation: React provides a stable set function for a state variable, so its identity does not change when the component re-renders.
